HP ProLiant ML10 Gen9 — Graphics / Display Fix (Linux, Windows Server & more)

Symptom: the onboard Intel graphics (HD Graphics P530, 8086:191d) works fine under nomodeset only at a fixed 1024×768, but as soon as you remove nomodeset — or on Windows Server — the display goes black / “no signal”. This repository is the complete, tested, documented fix: root-cause analysis, ready-to-run scripts for many distributions, Windows Server instructions, hardware/cable alternatives, and full troubleshooting.

Tested reference machine: HPE ProLiant ML10 Gen9, Xeon E3-1225 v5, 2× DisplayPort 1.2, monitor over DP → DVI → HDMI, Linux Mint 22.x. Result: 1366×768 @ 60 Hz with full hardware acceleration.

📄 New here? Read QUICKSTART.md first. 🖨️ Printable / offline: docs/dist/ProLiant-ML10-Graphics-fix.pdf (all documentation in one 49-page PDF) — see Screenshots.

TL;DR — the fix

The machine needs i915 (the Intel KMS driver) to own the display, and the output must be force-enabled because the DP→DVI→HDMI adapter chain does not pass EDID reliably:

# Linux kernel command line (remove nomodeset, add):
i915.enable_dc=0 i915.enable_psr=0 i915.enable_fbc=0 \
i915.enable_dp_mst=0 i915.disable_power_well=0 \
video=HDMI-A-1:1366x768@60e

Run the toolkit and let it do it for you:

./scripts/linux/i915-display-fix.sh status      # inspect
./scripts/linux/i915-display-fix.sh detect      # find your connector + mode
sudo ./scripts/linux/i915-display-fix.sh apply  # apply permanently
sudo reboot

On Windows Server / Windows there is no kernel command line — you install the Intel graphics driver and (if needed) use an active DisplayPort adapter. See docs/06-windows-server.md.

Why this repository exists

The ML10 Gen9 is a cheap, quiet Xeon tower with two DisplayPort 1.2 outputs on the motherboard and no HDMI. Most people connect a monitor meant for HDMI through a cheap DP→DVI→HDMI (or DP→HDMI) adapter. The result is a machine that “has no video” under a real graphics driver. Every forum answer says one of:

  • “Use nomodeset” → you get 1024×768 forever and no GPU acceleration;
  • “Use an active adapter” → correct, but nobody explains why, or how to make a passive one work;
  • “The ML10 has no iGPU support” → false, the P530 is fully supported.

This repository documents the actual technical cause and gives a software fix that works with a passive adapter, plus the hardware fix if you prefer it, on every OS we could test or verify.

Safety

  • Every script is non-destructive by default and keeps timestamped backups (/var/backups/i915-display-fix/).
  • A guaranteed recovery boot entry (nomodeset) is always left in place, so a bad change is never permanent.
  • apply --dry-run shows exactly what will change and touches nothing.

⚠️ The scripts edit the bootloader configuration. Read the relevant docs first, and keep a way to reach a console (physical keyboard or SSH enabled beforehand) if you are changing display settings on a machine you cannot see.

QUICKSTART

The 60‑second version. Full detail lives in docs/ and README.md.

What this fixes

HP ProLiant ML10 Gen9 (Intel HD Graphics P530) shows no signal / black screen, or is stuck at a fixed 1024×768, when the monitor is connected through the motherboard's DisplayPort via a DP → DVI → HDMI adapter.

Cause: the passive adapter hides the monitor's EDID, so the driver never enables the output. nomodeset "works" only by abandoning the GPU entirely.

Linux — 3 commands

cd scripts/linux
./i915-display-fix.sh detect                 # tells you the connector + mode
sudo ./i915-display-fix.sh apply             # applies it permanently
sudo reboot

If the screen is dark right now and you don't know the connector name:

sudo ./i915-display-fix.sh discover          # adds a safe "no nomodeset" GRUB entry
sudo reboot                                  # pick "i915 DISCOVER" at the menu
./i915-display-fix.sh detect                 # then apply with what it prints

Verify after rebooting:

./i915-display-fix.sh status

Revert any time:

sudo ./i915-display-fix.sh revert

The raw kernel parameters (any distro)

Remove nomodeset; add these to the kernel command line:

i915.enable_dc=0 i915.enable_psr=0 i915.enable_fbc=0 i915.enable_dp_mst=0 i915.disable_power_well=0 video=HDMI-A-1:1366x768@60e
  • Replace HDMI-A-1 with your connector (DP-1 if the monitor is native DP).
  • Replace 1366x768 with your monitor's native resolution.
  • Keep the trailing e (force-enable even when "disconnected").
  • Never force both DP-1 and HDMI-A-1 — they are the same physical port.

Per‑distro regeneration: see docs/05-distro-guide.md.

Windows / Windows Server

There is no kernel command line — install the Intel graphics driver and, if the monitor still isn't detected, use an active DP→HDMI adapter.

Fix-Display.bat info          :: are you on the Basic Display Adapter?
Fix-Display.bat list          :: supported modes
Fix-Display.bat set 1366 768  :: set + persist a mode
Fix-Display.bat best          :: highest mode the display reports

Full guide: docs/06-windows-server.md.

OS Quick fix

Proxmox / TrueNAS SCALE / Unraid Linux fix above
VMware ESXi manage over the network (no iGPU driver)

Details: docs/07-other-os.md.

Always works: the hardware fix

A passive DP→HDMI/DVI plug cannot pass EDID. An active one can, and then Linux, Windows and FreeBSD all just work — no software changes needed. See docs/08-hardware-cables-adapters.md.

Install the toolkit system‑wide (optional)

sudo ./install.sh        # installs to /usr/local/sbin
sudo i915-display-fix status

  • Still dark → docs/09-troubleshooting.md
  • Prove it worked → docs/10-verification.md
  • Collect a report to share → bash scripts/linux/i915-collect.sh /tmp/i915

1. Problem statement

1.1 Summary

On an HPE ProLiant ML10 Gen9 with the onboard Intel HD Graphics P530 (8086:191d), a monitor connected through the motherboard's DisplayPort — in practice nearly always via a DP → DVI → HDMI or DP → HDMI adapter — does not produce a picture under a normal Linux graphics stack.

Two distinct behaviours are reported:

Configuration Result
nomodeset on the kernel command line (the “safe” default) Boots to a fixed 1024×768 desktop. No GPU acceleration. Resolution cannot be changed in software.
nomodeset removed (“normal” boot) Black screen / “no signal” from the motherboard. Sometimes a dark mouse cursor flickers in a corner.
Windows Server / Windows Often no display at all after driver install, or a “generic” 640×480 desktop.

1.2 Why people hit this

The ML10 Gen9 motherboard exposes two DisplayPort 1.2 connectors and no HDMI/DVI/VGA. The overwhelming majority of monitors in this price bracket are HDMI. So the realistic chain is:

[motherboard DP] ──► [DP→DVI plug] ──► [DVI→HDMI cable] ──► [monitor HDMI]

At least three things are wrong with that chain on this hardware:

  1. nomodeset is not a resolution fix — it disables kernel mode-setting entirely, leaving you with the firmware’s fixed framebuffer.
  2. EDID (the monitor’s “capabilities chip”) is not passed reliably through cheap passive adapters, so the driver cannot see that a monitor is attached.
  3. On Intel, a dual-mode (“DP++”) port appears twice: once under its DP name (DP-1) and once under its HDMI name (HDMI-A-1). Force-enabling the wrong one, or both, makes the driver fight itself.

1.3 Scope of this repository

In scope:

  • Every Linux distribution we can cover with a bootloader-based fix (GRUB and systemd-boot), including per-distro commands.
  • Windows Server 2012 R2 → 2025 and Windows 10/11.
  • FreeBSD and the common virtualisation/“NAS” platforms.
  • Hardware alternatives (active adapters, KVMs, alternative connectors).

Out of scope (documented only):

  • Reflashing the BIOS/firmware.
  • Adding a discrete GPU.
  • Multi-monitor tiling edge cases.

2. Diagnosis & evidence

This is the actual investigation that produced the fix, in order, with the real commands and their outputs. You can reproduce every step on your own ML10.

2.1 Identify the GPU and driver

$ lspci -nnk | grep -A3 -iE 'VGA|Display'
00:02.0 VGA compatible controller [0300]: Intel Corporation HD Graphics P530 [8086:191d] (rev 06)
        DeviceName:  Onboard IGD
        Subsystem: Intel Corporation HD Graphics P530 [8086:2212]
        Kernel driver in use: i915

So the hardware is supported by i915. (00:02.0 is the standard location of the Intel iGPU.)

2.2 Confirm what is actually driving the display

$ cat /proc/cmdline
... ro quiet splash nomodeset
$ grep -w i915 /proc/modules || echo "i915 NOT loaded"
i915 NOT loaded
$ lsmod | grep -E 'i915|simpledrm'
simpledrm    ...

With nomodeset, only the firmware framebuffer (simpledrm) is active. That is why the resolution is fixed and unchangeable: nothing is programming the CRTC.

2.3 Prove that nomodeset is the blocker

$ sudo modprobe i915
modprobe: ERROR: could not insert 'i915': No such device

i915 refuses to bind while nomodeset is active — it is not a missing driver, it is a kernel policy flag (video_firmware_drivers_only()), and it is boot-time only. No amount of rmmod/modprobe will fix it; you must change the kernel command line and reboot.

2.4 Look at the connector the firmware left enabled

Booting once without nomodeset and with verbose DRM logging (drm.debug=0x1e) makes i915 speak. Two things jump out.

(a) The port really is dual-mode

i915 ... [drm:intel_bios_init] Port B VBT info: CRT:0 DVI:1 HDMI:1 DP:1 DP++:1
i915 ... [drm:intel_bios_init] Port C VBT info: CRT:0 DVI:1 HDMI:1 DP:1 DP++:1
i915 ... [drm:intel_bios_init] Port D VBT info: CRT:0 DVI:1 HDMI:1 DP:1 DP++:1

DP++:1 on ports B/C/D means the GPU can emit TMDS (DVI/HDMI) through a passive adapter. The adapter is not the (only) problem.

(b) EDID does not come through cleanly

i915 ... [drm:intel_hdmi_set_edid] HDMI GMBUS EDID read failed, retry using GPIO bit-banging
i915 ... [drm:intel_hdmi_set_edid] HDMI GMBUS EDID read failed, retry using GPIO bit-banging
...

Hundreds of these. The GMBUS (hardware DDC) read fails; the kernel falls back to bit-banging the DDC lines, which is slow and racy at boot. If it loses the race, the connector is treated as “disconnected” and the output stays dark.

(c) A dual-mode port has TWO names

i915 ... [drm:intel_dp_init_connector]   Adding DP connector on [ENCODER:109:DDI B/PHY B]
i915 ... [drm:intel_hdmi_init_connector] Adding HDMI connector on [ENCODER:109:DDI B/PHY B]
...
i915 ... [CONNECTOR:120:HDMI-A-1] hw state readout: enabled

DP-1 and HDMI-A-1 are the same physical port (DDI B). The BIOS left HDMI-A-1 enabled, i.e. that is the connector your cable is on.

2.5 The first, wrong “fix” — and why it failed

Forcing all candidate connectors:

video=DP-1:1366x768@60e video=DP-2:1366x768@60e \
video=HDMI-A-1:1366x768@60e video=HDMI-A-2:1366x768@60e

produced “signal, but a black screen with a flickering cursor”. The kernel explains why:

i915 ... [drm:handle_conflicting_encoders] [ENCODER:109:DDI B/PHY B] in use on
        [CRTC:58:pipe A], disabling [CONNECTOR:120:HDMI-A-1]
i915 ... [drm:update_connector_routing] Disabling [CONNECTOR:110:DP-1]

DP-1 grabbed the DDI B encoder, so the driver kept disabling the real monitor (HDMI-A-1). Xorg then saw four outputs (two of them phantom) and set them all to 640×480 — hence black screen, occasional cursor.

2.6 The correct fix

Force only the connector that matches the cable:

video=HDMI-A-1:1366x768@60e

Result on the reference machine:

$ cat /proc/cmdline
... quiet splash i915.enable_dc=0 i915.enable_psr=0 i915.enable_fbc=0 \
    i915.enable_dp_mst=0 i915.disable_power_well=0 video=HDMI-A-1:1366x768@60e

$ head -1 /sys/class/drm/card1-HDMI-A-1/modes
1366x768
$ xrandr | grep connected
HDMI-1 connected primary 1366x768+0+0 ...
$ glxinfo | grep 'OpenGL renderer'
OpenGL renderer string: Mesa Intel(R) HD Graphics P530 (SKL GT2)

3. Root cause

Four independent facts combine into the failure. Understanding them tells you which fix will work and which will not.

3.1 nomodeset is a global, boot-time kill switch

nomodeset sets the kernel variable video_firmware_drivers_only(). While it is set, DRM/KMS drivers are not allowed to take over the display; only the firmware’s simple framebuffer (simpledrm, driven by the BIOS GOP) is used.

Consequences:

  • Resolution is whatever the firmware set at boot — here 1024×768 — and cannot be changed.
  • No hardware acceleration; the desktop runs on software rendering (llvmpipe).
  • modprobe i915 fails with No such device (the driver declines to probe).
  • It cannot be undone at runtime. It is read once at boot.
flowchart LR
  A[kernel cmdline] -->|has nomodeset| B[video_firmware_drivers_only = true]
  B --> C[i915 refuses to bind]
  C --> D[simpledrm / fixed 1024x768]
  A -->|no nomodeset| E[i915 binds]
  E --> F[KMS: real modes, acceleration]

3.2 EDID does not survive the DP→DVI→HDMI chain

EDID is the small data block a monitor exposes over the DDC channel (I²C). The driver needs it to know the monitor exists and what modes it supports.

On Intel, DDC is normally read through GMBUS (a hardware I²C controller). Cheap passive adapters — and even some active ones — break or degrade DDC, so:

intel_hdmi_set_edid: HDMI GMBUS EDID read failed, retry using GPIO bit-banging

appears hundreds of times. The fallback (bit-banging GPIO) is slow and, during early boot, often loses the race with the desktop starting. When that happens the connector is reported disconnected → the output is never turned on → “no signal”.

This is why the hardware fix is “use an active adapter” (it regenerates DDC), and why the software fix is “force the connector on and tell the driver the mode” so it does not need EDID at all.

3.3 A dual-mode (DP++) port has two names

Intel DP++ ports can carry native DisplayPort or TMDS (DVI/HDMI) depending on what is plugged in. Because of that, the driver registers two connectors on one physical port, e.g.:

port DDI B ──┬── connector DP-1        (native DP)
             └── connector HDMI-A-1    (DP++ / TMDS)

The BIOS leaves the one matching the actual cable enabled. On the reference machine hd state readout: enabled was on HDMI-A-1, so the cable is on the DP++ path in HDMI mode.

Trap: force-enabling both names makes two connectors share one encoder:

handle_conflicting_encoders: [DDI B/PHY B] in use on pipe A, disabling HDMI-A-1

…and the driver disables the real monitor in a loop. This produces the notorious “signal present, black screen, flashing cursor”.

3.4 Skylake-era power management can blank an output

Skylake’s display engine has aggressive power features that are known to cause black screens / flicker on external adapters:

  • DC states (display C-states) — i915.enable_dc
  • PSR (Panel Self Refresh) — i915.enable_psr
  • FBC (Frame Buffer Compression) — i915.enable_fbc
  • Power wells — i915.disable_power_well

Disabling them (as this repo does) trades a little idle power for stability. On a desktop/server that is the right trade.

3.5 Minimal working condition

Putting it together, the display lights up iff all of these are true:

  1. nomodeset is absent (so i915 binds).
  2. The correct connector name is force-enabled (video=<name>:<mode>e), compensating for the missing EDID.
  3. A supported mode is requested (here 1366×768@60).
  4. Optionally, Skylake power features are disabled for stability.

Note that (2) is only necessary because of (3.2). With a good active adapter, plain boot without video= usually works, because EDID is readable.

4. Linux solution (the fix)

This document is the canonical, step-by-step procedure. It assumes GRUB (the default on Ubuntu/Mint/Debian/Fedora/Arch/openSUSE); systemd-boot and distro-specific commands are in 05-distro-guide.md.

Two ways to run it: the automated toolkit (scripts/linux/i915-display-fix.sh), or the manual steps below. Both do exactly the same thing.

4.1 Automated (recommended)

cd scripts/linux
chmod +x i915-display-fix.sh

# 1. Inspect the current state (read-only, safe):
./i915-display-fix.sh status

# 2. If i915 is running, it can tell you the connector + mode:
./i915-display-fix.sh detect
#    -> "Apply it with: sudo ./i915-display-fix.sh apply --connector HDMI-A-1 --mode 1366x768"

# 3. Preview, then apply:
sudo ./i915-display-fix.sh apply --dry-run
sudo ./i915-display-fix.sh apply

# 4. Reboot (do NOT touch the menu; it auto-boots the fixed entry):
sudo reboot

If the machine is currently dark and you do not know the connector name, use the two-phase workflow in 09-troubleshooting.md.

4.2 Manual (GRUB) — the exact steps

Step 1 — Find the connector name

If you can already boot to a desktop with nomodeset, you still cannot see the real connector name (only Unknown-1 from simpledrm). The reliable way is to boot once without nomodeset and read the state, even if the screen is dark:

# after booting without nomodeset, over SSH or a second console:
for c in /sys/class/drm/*/status; do
  echo "$(basename "$(dirname "$c")"): $(cat "$c")"
done

You want the connector whose status is connected — typically HDMI-A-1 or DP-1. (If nothing is connected, see the discover workflow.)

Step 2 — Edit /etc/default/grub

sudo cp -a /etc/default/grub /etc/default/grub.bak-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)
sudo nano /etc/default/grub

Change the line:

-GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT="quiet splash nomodeset"
+GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT="quiet splash i915.enable_dc=0 i915.enable_psr=0 i915.enable_fbc=0 i915.enable_dp_mst=0 i915.disable_power_well=0 video=HDMI-A-1:1366x768@60e"

Notes:

  • Delete nomodeset.
  • HDMI-A-1 → your connector name from Step 1.
  • 1366x768 → your monitor’s native resolution (see 10-verification.md).
  • Keep the e suffix (force-enable even if “disconnected”).

Optional, to make the menu visible long enough to reach a recovery entry:

+GRUB_TIMEOUT_STYLE=menu
+GRUB_TIMEOUT=10

Step 3 — Regenerate the GRUB config

Debian/Ubuntu/Mint:

sudo update-grub

Fedora/RHEL/openSUSE:

sudo grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg

Arch:

sudo grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg

Step 4 — Add a recovery entry (strongly recommended)

Create /etc/grub.d/42_i915_fix_recovery (mode 0755) so you always have a one-keystroke way back to a working 1024×768 desktop:

KREL=$(uname -r)
UUID=$(findmnt -no UUID /)
sudo tee /etc/grub.d/42_i915_fix_recovery >/dev/null <<EOF
#!/bin/sh
exec tail -n +3 \$0
menuentry "Recovery - safe graphics (nomodeset)" --class gnu-linux --class os {
    recordfail
    load_video
    set gfxpayload=keep
    insmod gzio
    insmod part_gpt
    insmod ext2
    search --no-floppy --fs-uuid --set=root $UUID
    linux  /boot/vmlinuz-$KREL root=UUID=$UUID ro quiet splash nomodeset
    initrd /boot/initrd.img-$KREL
}
EOF
sudo chmod 755 /etc/grub.d/42_i915_fix_recovery
sudo update-grub

⚠️ Never leave *.bak copies inside /etc/grub.d/. GRUB executes every executable file in that directory, and a backup containing a menuentry line becomes a duplicate menu entry. Keep backups in /root/ or /var/backups/.

Step 5 — Reboot and verify

sudo reboot
# after it comes back:
cat /proc/cmdline
xrandr | grep connected         # expect "<name> connected primary 1366x768+0+0"

4.3 What each parameter does

Parameter Effect Why it is here
(remove) nomodeset Lets i915 bind The essential change
video=HDMI-A-1:1366x768@60e Force-enable connector + mode Works around missing EDID
i915.enable_dc=0 Disable display C-states Skylake analog power glitches
i915.enable_psr=0 Disable Panel Self Refresh No panel here; avoids blanking
i915.enable_fbc=0 Disable frame-buffer compression Avoids flicker on adapters
i915.enable_dp_mst=0 Disable DP Multi-Stream No MST hub; simplifies link setup
i915.disable_power_well=0 Keep power wells always on Maximum stability

Only nomodeset-removal and the video= token are strictly required in most cases. The i915.* flags are belt-and-braces stability; drop them if you prefer default power behaviour and it still works.

4.4 Reverting

sudo cp -a /etc/default/grub.bak-<timestamp> /etc/default/grub
sudo rm -f /etc/grub.d/42_i915_fix_recovery
sudo update-grub
sudo reboot

Or with the toolkit:

sudo ./i915-display-fix.sh revert

4.5 Changing the resolution later

Temporarily (current session):

xrandr --output HDMI-1 --mode 1366x768

Permanently: change 1366x768 in the video= token and re-run Step 3, or add an Xorg configuration / a desktop startup command (see 05-distro-guide.md).

5. Distribution & bootloader guide

The toolkit edits the bootloader, so one script covers every GRUB-based and systemd-boot-based distribution. status and detect are read-only and safe everywhere; apply/revert/discover need root.

OS / family Versions covered Bootloader Regeneration command
Ubuntu / Linux Mint / Pop!_OS / elementary / Zorin 20.04, 22.04, 24.04, LM 20–22 GRUB update-grub
Debian 10, 11, 12, 13 GRUB update-grub
Fedora / RHEL / CentOS Stream / Rocky / Alma 8, 9, 10 GRUB2 grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg
Arch / Manjaro / EndeavourOS rolling GRUB or systemd-boot grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg
openSUSE Leap / Tumbleweed / SLES 15.x GRUB2 grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg
NixOS any GRUB/systemd-boot declarative (configuration.nix)
Void / Gentoo / Alpine any various manual

The script auto-detects the distribution (/etc/os-release), the correct regeneration tool, and the GRUB config path. Kernel version does not matter — only uname -r is used to locate the image for the optional recovery entry.

5.1 Ubuntu / Linux Mint / Debian / Pop!_OS

./i915-display-fix.sh detect
sudo ./i915-display-fix.sh apply --connector HDMI-A-1 --mode 1366x768
sudo reboot

Equivalent manual edit of /etc/default/grub:

GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT="quiet splash i915.enable_dc=0 i915.enable_psr=0 i915.enable_fbc=0 i915.enable_dp_mst=0 i915.disable_power_well=0 video=HDMI-A-1:1366x768@60e"

then sudo update-grub.

5.2 Fedora / RHEL / Rocky / AlmaLinux / CentOS Stream

sudo ./i915-display-fix.sh apply --connector HDMI-A-1 --mode 1366x768
# or, the distro-native way:
sudo grubby --update-kernel=ALL --remove-args=nomodeset \
  --args='i915.enable_dc=0 i915.enable_psr=0 i915.enable_fbc=0 i915.enable_dp_mst=0 i915.disable_power_well=0 video=HDMI-A-1:1366x768@60e'
  • UEFI and BIOS both work. The GRUB config on UEFI Fedora is still /boot/grub2/grub.cfg (the EFI/fedora/grub.cfg file is a stub that loads it).
  • grubby is present on RHEL-family systems and is the safest option; it edits all kernel entries at once.
  • After a kernel update, grubby --update-kernel=ALL persists, but a plain grub2-mkconfig edit of /etc/default/grub also persists. Both are fine.

5.3 Arch / Manjaro / EndeavourOS

Detect which bootloader you use:

[ -d /boot/loader/entries ] && echo systemd-boot || echo grub

GRUB:

sudo ./i915-display-fix.sh apply --connector HDMI-A-1 --mode 1366x768

systemd-boot (the toolkit edits /boot/loader/entries/*.conf):

sudo ./i915-display-fix.sh apply --connector HDMI-A-1 --mode 1366x768

Manual equivalent — edit the options line of your entry, e.g. /boot/loader/entries/arch.conf:

options root=UUID=... rw quiet i915.enable_dc=0 i915.enable_psr=0 i915.enable_fbc=0 i915.enable_dp_mst=0 i915.disable_power_well=0 video=HDMI-A-1:1366x768@60e

Add a recovery entry by copying the file and appending nomodeset:

sudo cp /boot/loader/entries/arch.conf /boot/loader/entries/arch-recovery.conf
sudo sed -i 's/$/ nomodeset/' /boot/loader/entries/arch-recovery.conf

5.4 openSUSE Leap / Tumbleweed / SLES

sudo ./i915-display-fix.sh apply --connector HDMI-A-1 --mode 1366x768
# manual:
sudo sed -i 's/^GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT=.*/GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT="... video=HDMI-A-1:1366x768@60e"/' /etc/default/grub
sudo grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg

YaST → Boot Loader → Kernel Parameters also works if you prefer a GUI.

5.5 NixOS (declarative — the script cannot edit it safely)

In /etc/nixos/configuration.nix:

{
  boot.kernelParams = [
    "i915.enable_dc=0"
    "i915.enable_psr=0"
    "i915.enable_fbc=0"
    "i915.enable_dp_mst=0"
    "i915.disable_power_well=0"
    "video=HDMI-A-1:1366x768@60e"
  ];
  # keep several generations so you can roll back at the boot menu
  boot.loader.grub.configurationLimit = 10;
  # never put "nomodeset" here:
  # boot.kernelParams = [ "nomodeset" ];   # <-- do NOT do this
}

Then sudo nixos-rebuild switch. Roll back with nixos-rebuild switch --rollback or by picking an older generation in the boot menu.

5.6 Void / Gentoo / Alpine and other bootloaders

apply prints the parameters to use and leaves the bootloader alone when it does not recognise it. Add these to your kernel command line:

i915.enable_dc=0 i915.enable_psr=0 i915.enable_fbc=0 i915.enable_dp_mst=0 i915.disable_power_well=0 video=HDMI-A-1:1366x768@60e
  • Void: /etc/default/grub + sudo update-grub (same as Debian), or edit /boot/loader/entries/ for systemd-boot.
  • Gentoo: often a hand-written /boot/grub/grub.cfg; append the parameters to the linux line.
  • Alpine: /etc/update-extlinux.conf (extlinux) or the GRUB config; append to default_kernel_opts / the kernel line.
  • rEFInd: edit /boot/refind_linux.conf.

Persisting the resolution in X

The video= force sets the mode at boot, which is usually enough for GDM/SDDM/LightDM. If your desktop still starts at a lower mode, pin it per-user or system-wide.

Per-user (all desktops): add a desktop autostart script:

mkdir -p ~/.config/autostart
cat > ~/.config/autostart/i915-resolution.desktop <<'EOF'
[Desktop Entry]
Type=Application
Name=Set 1366x768
Exec=sh -c "sleep 3; xrandr --output HDMI-1 --mode 1366x768 || xrandr --output HDMI-1 --auto"
X-GNOME-Autostart-enabled=true
EOF

System-wide (Xorg, all users): /etc/X11/xorg.conf.d/20-i915-mode.conf:

Section "Monitor"
    Identifier "HDMI-1"
    Option "PreferredMode" "1366x768"
EndSection

(Requires the modesetting driver, which is the default for Intel.)

Wayland (GNOME/KDE): the kernel video= mode is honoured at boot; change the mode from the desktop’s Display settings.

6. Windows Server & Windows (10/11)

Windows does not use a kernel command line, so the Linux fix does not apply. The same machine, cable chain and failure show up differently here, and the solution is a combination of driver and hardware work.

6.1 Why Windows Server shows no/ugly video on this box

  1. Windows Server ships a generic driver. Until a real graphics driver is installed, Windows uses the Microsoft Basic Display Adapter (msbasicdisplay). That adapter: - ignores most of the GPU, - caps the mode list to what the firmware/EDID provides, - with a passive DP→DVI→HDMI chain that hides EDID, often leaves you at 640×480 or 1024×768.

  2. Intel does not officially support consumer iGPUs on Windows Server. There is no SKU of the HD Graphics P530 driver labelled “Windows Server 2022”. The Windows 10/11 64-bit driver can usually still be installed manually (“Have Disk”), but you must bypass the compatibility check.

  3. The same EDID problem as Linux. The DP++ port is fine, but a passive adapter can drop the DDC channel, so Windows cannot read the monitor. This is the root of “640×480 only” and “no signal”.

Practical consequence: on Windows the single most effective fix is an active DisplayPort adapter (see 08-hardware-cables-adapters.md). Driver installation gets you acceleration and correct modes; the adapter fixes detection.

6.2 Solution A — install the Intel graphics driver (recommended first step)

What you need

Item Value
GPU Intel HD Graphics P530, VEN_8086&DEV_191D
Last Windows 10/11 x64 driver for Skylake (Gen9) Intel 15.45.x series, e.g. 15.45.34.5174, INF name igdlh64.inf
Alternative Intel DCH driver 31.0.101.x (Skylake support is limited/vendor-specific)
HP option Search HP support for “ML10 Gen9 Intel Graphics” SoftPaq (may cover Win Server 2012 R2/2016)

Method 1 — Device Manager “Have Disk” (works on Server 2016/2019/2022)

  1. Download and extract the Intel driver package (.exe → run it and let it extract to C:\SWSetup\..., or use 7-Zip; the .inf files are in a subfolder such as Graphics).
  2. Device Manager → Display adapters → Microsoft Basic Display Adapter → Update driver → Browse my computer → Let me pick from a list → Have Disk…
  3. Point to igdlh64.inf in the extracted folder.
  4. Choose Intel(R) HD Graphics P530 (or 530) and accept the compatibility warning.
  5. Reboot. Verify:
Get-CimInstance Win32_VideoController |
  Select-Object Name, DriverVersion, CurrentHorizontalResolution, CurrentVerticalResolution

You want Intel(R) HD Graphics ... and your native resolution, not Microsoft Basic Display Adapter.

If the INF refuses to install on Server 2022/2025 because of the OS version, either (a) use the Windows 10/11 driver of the same WDDM generation, or (b) temporarily enable test signing / driver signature enforcement bypass, install, then re-enable. Prefer (a).

Method 2 — pnputil (scriptable, no GUI)

# Stage and install the INF (admin PowerShell):
pnputil /add-driver "C:\Drivers\Intel\Graphics\igdlh64.inf" /install
# If it installs as a package but does not bind:
pnputil /enum-drivers | Select-String -Context 0,4 igdlh
# then assign it in Device Manager, or:
Get-PnpDevice -Class Display | Enable-PnpDevice -Confirm:$false

scripts/windows/Install-IntelGraphicsDriver.ps1 automates the staging and points out the manual Device Manager step if binding is refused.

Method 3 — HP SoftPaq

HP occasionally publishes a Windows Server graphics driver for the ML10 Gen9 (usually for Server 2012 R2/2016). Check HP support by serial number; if it exists it installs cleanly with no compatibility hacks.

6.3 Solution B — fix detection (the EDID problem)

Even with the right driver, a passive adapter can leave Windows unable to read the monitor. In order of preference:

  1. Use an active DP adapter (see §6.4). This is the real fix and also helps Linux.
  2. Force a mode in the registry. Windows stores display configuration under:

HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\GraphicsDrivers\Configuration

Each subkey holds a PrimSurfSize.cx / PrimSurfSize.cy and per-monitor ActiveSize.cx / .cy. Setting them to 1366 / 768 and rebooting will make Windows try that mode (it only sticks if the adapter/EDID allows it). Back up the key first. This is a workaround, not a guarantee. 3. Set the mode at logon with a script (see §6.5). Works when the mode exists in the list but Windows picks a lower one.

6.4 Solution C — hardware: the active adapter

HP documents that the ML10 Gen9 DisplayPorts expect an active DP adapter. Active adapters contain a level-shifter/converter chip (DisplayPort → TMDS) and regenerate DDC, so both Windows and Linux see a proper monitor.

Buy one of:

  • Active DP → HDMI (the cleanest: one cable), or
  • Active DP → DVI, then a DVI→HDMI cable.

Look for the words “active” / “DP++ to HDMI active” in the product listing. A passive “DP to HDMI” plug has no chip and will reproduce this exact bug.

See 08-hardware-cables-adapters.md for details and alternatives.

6.5 Registry / PowerShell resolution control

Built-in (some Server versions)

Get-DisplayResolution           # if the cmdlet exists
Set-DisplayResolution -Width 1366 -Height 768

(These cmdlets exist on Server Core in several Server releases; if Get-Command cannot find them, use the next method.)

Portable (works on every Windows / Server)

Use the provided scripts:

# inventory: GPU, driver, monitors, and every mode each output supports
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\windows\Get-GraphicsInfo.ps1

# list modes, then set one (uses ChangeDisplaySettingsEx via P/Invoke)
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\windows\Set-DisplayResolution.ps1 -List
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\windows\Set-DisplayResolution.ps1 -Width 1366 -Height 768

Or the tiny native tool (see §6.6):

DisplayFix.exe --list
DisplayFix.exe --set 1366 768
DisplayFix.exe --best

Third-party CLIs (if you prefer)

  • QRes (Anders Kjersem): QRes.exe /x:1366 /y:768
  • NirCmd (NirSoft): nircmd.exe setdisplay 1366 768 32
  • DisplayChanger (12noon): dc64.exe -width=1366 -height=768

These are convenient for logon scripts / Task Scheduler “At log on”.

6.6 The DisplayFix.exe native tool

Because a native binary is handy for logon scripts, unattended setups and Server Core, this repo includes its source and a build recipe:

scripts/windows/src/DisplayFix.c      # ~200 lines, Win32 only, no dependencies

Features: - --list — enumerate adapters and every supported mode. - --set W H [Hz] [device] — apply a mode and persist it (CDS_UPDATEREGISTRY). - --best [Hz] [device] — pick the highest mode the adapter reports. - --current — print the active mode.

Build it (on any Linux with mingw-w64)

sudo apt-get install -y mingw-w64        # Debian/Ubuntu
make windows                              # produces scripts/windows/DisplayFix.exe

or directly:

x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc -O2 -municode -o DisplayFix.exe src/DisplayFix.c -lgdi32 -luser32

Build it on Windows

:: With Visual Studio (Developer Command Prompt):
cl /O2 /DUNICODE /D_UNICODE DisplayFix.c user32.lib gdi32.lib /Fe:DisplayFix.exe
:: With MinGW-w64 for Windows:
gcc -O2 -municode -o DisplayFix.exe DisplayFix.c -lgdi32 -luser32

The repository ships the source; a pre-built binary may or may not be present depending on whether it was built (see scripts/windows/README.md). If absent, build it with the two commands above, or just use the PowerShell scripts, which need no compiler.

6.7 Headless / remote servers

If the ML10 runs as a headless server, the physical console mode is mostly irrelevant — use RDP, which renders at the client’s resolution regardless of the local adapter:

  • Enable: Server Manager → Local Server → Remote Desktop, or powershell Set-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server' -Name fDenyTSConnections -Value 0 Enable-NetFirewallRule -DisplayGroup "Remote Desktop"
  • For a server with no desktop experience and no GPU driver, RDP still gives you a usable desktop at your chosen size.

6.8 Windows 10 / 11 (workstation)

Simpler than Server:

  1. Let Windows Update install a graphics driver, or run the Intel Driver & Support Assistant.
  2. If the monitor is not detected through a passive adapter, install an active DP adapter.
  3. Resolution: Settings → System → Display, or DisplayFix.exe --best.

Windows 10/11 have full WDDM support and hardware acceleration for the P530 with the 15.45 or newer driver.

6.9 Windows checklist

  • [ ] Confirm Ven_8086&Dev_191D is present (Device Manager → Details → Hardware Ids).
  • [ ] Install a real Intel driver (no more “Microsoft Basic Display Adapter”).
  • [ ] Confirm EDID is read (monitor shows a name in Display settings, not “Generic PnP Monitor”).
  • [ ] If not, replace the passive adapter with an active one.
  • [ ] Pin the resolution (Display settings / script / DisplayFix.exe).
  • [ ] For unattended servers, prefer RDP and ignore the physical console.

7. Other operating systems

The root causes (EDID over a passive adapter; no nomodeset concept elsewhere) recur on every OS. Below is what to do on the platforms people actually run on an ML10 Gen9-class box.

7.1 FreeBSD

FreeBSD uses the i915kms kernel module (a port of the Linux driver). There is no nomodeset.

# /boot/loader.conf
i915kms_load="YES"
kern.vty=vt                 # use the new vt(4) console

Load immediately without rebooting:

kldload i915kms

Check:

pciconf -lv | grep -A4 vgapci
sysctl kern.vty
dmesg | grep -i i915

If the monitor is not detected through the adapter, force the mode:

# after X starts, or from a script:
xrandr                 # list outputs (often HDMI-1 / DP-1)
xrandr --output HDMI-1 --mode 1366x768

FreeBSD has no video= kernel token; use an active adapter for reliable detection, or an /etc/X11/xorg.conf.d/ PreferredMode stanza as in Linux.

A helper is provided: scripts/freebsd/i915-freebsd.sh.

7.2 Proxmox VE / Debian hypervisor

Proxmox is Debian under the hood → the Linux fix applies directly:

sudo ./scripts/linux/i915-display-fix.sh apply --connector HDMI-A-1 --mode 1366x768
sudo reboot

If the host is headless, the local console barely matters; the fix is mainly so the boot console and any local login are usable.

7.3 VMware ESXi

ESXi is a hypervisor, not a desktop. The integrated GPU is not used; ESXi runs a VGA/EFI framebuffer at low resolution for its DCUI (“yellow console”). This is by design — you manage ESXi over the network (Host Client / vSphere).

  • If the DCUI is unreadable through an adapter, add an active adapter or use IPMI/remote management.
  • Passing the iGPU to a VM (GTV-d / Intel GVT-g) is not supported on Skylake P530 in ESXi’s standard tooling; use a discrete GPU for that.

7.4 TrueNAS SCALE / CORE, Unraid, OMV

All are Linux:

  • TrueNAS SCALE / Unraid / OMV (Debian/RHEL-derived): run the Linux toolkit. On TrueNAS SCALE the root filesystem is managed, but kernel parameters can be added via the UI (System → Advanced → Kernel command line / sysctl) or /etc/default/grub + update-grub from a shell.
  • TrueNAS CORE (FreeBSD): follow §7.1.

For appliance-style NAS boxes with no keyboard/video session, the practical fix is again the active adapter.

7.5 pfSense / OPNsense (FreeBSD)

Same as FreeBSD (§7.1): load i915kms, and force the mode if needed. These router images are usually headless; the console is only used once.

7.6 illumos / OpenIndiana / SmartOS

Intel KMS support is limited/experimental. On Skylake P530 expect the generic VGA framebuffer. Use an active adapter, and drive the machine over the network. Not a supported display target.

7.7 ChromeOS Flex / other Linux appliances

ChromeOS Flex uses the standard Intel graphics stack. Boot parameters are not user-editable in the usual way; rely on the active adapter.

7.8 Dual-boot / multi-OS on the same machine

Because the fix is per-OS, you can run Linux (fixed via kernel line) and Windows/Server (fixed via driver + adapter) side by side on the ML10 Gen9. The active adapter benefits every OS at once and is the recommended baseline.

7.9 Summary table

OS Mechanism Best fix
Linux (any distro) i915 + video= on kernel cmdline This repo’s toolkit
Windows / Server Intel WDDM driver Driver + active adapter
FreeBSD / pfSense / TrueNAS CORE i915kms i915kms_load=YES (+ active adapter)
Proxmox / TrueNAS SCALE / Unraid Linux Linux toolkit
ESXi hypervisor framebuffer only Manage over network; active adapter for DCUI
illumos limited KMS active adapter, manage over network

8. Hardware, cables, adapters & alternative solutions

Sometimes the cleanest fix is physical. This document explains the options and why they work.

8.1 What the ML10 Gen9 actually has

The motherboard has 2 × DisplayPort 1.2 and no HDMI/DVI/VGA. Per the GPU VBT (see examples/i915-vbt-ports.txt), ports B/C/D are DP++ (dual-mode), i.e. they can emit native DisplayPort or TMDS (DVI/HDMI) signals.

Two implications:

  1. A passive DP→HDMI/DVI adapter is electrically allowed (DP++), which is why the machine sometimes gives a picture at all.
  2. But passive adapters have no chip to regenerate DDC/EDID, so detection is unreliable → the failure in this repo.

HP’s own documentation for the ML10 Gen9 states the DP ports require an active dongle. This is the “official” hardware answer.

8.2 Passive vs active adapters

Passive DP→HDMI/DVI Active DP→HDMI/DVI
Chip inside none level shifter / protocol converter
Works when source is DP++ sometimes always
Passes EDID/DDC reliably often no yes
Fixes this bug no yes
Linux video= workaround needed yes usually not

How to tell them apart: active adapters are usually slightly larger, contain a chip, are labelled “active”, “DP++ to HDMI”, or explicitly “for NVIDIA/AMD/ non-DP++”. A “DP to HDMI passive” plug is the one causing trouble.

8.3 Recommended cables/adapters

In rough order of preference:

  1. Active DP → HDMI cable/adapter, then a normal HDMI cable to the monitor. One hop, EDID regenerated, works on the ML10 out of the box.
  2. Active DP → DVI, then DVI→HDMI cable. Also fine; two hops but the active DP→DVI regenerates DDC.
  3. Active DP → VGA (if you must drive a VGA monitor; degrades quality).
  4. USB graphics adapter (DisplayLink) — an entirely different path that bypasses the iGPU output; requires drivers on every OS.
  5. A monitor with DisplayPort — remove the adapters entirely; the cleanest of all if you are buying hardware.

Avoid: passive DP→HDMI/DVI plugs, “DP to HDMI” cables with no chip, unpowered KVMs with DP inputs that do not support DP++.

8.4 KVM switches

Many KVM switches present a fake EDID to the computer so switching does not disturb the display. That is actually helpful here (it removes the EDID race). Caveats:

  • A KVM that does not emulate EDID behaves like a bad adapter.
  • Prefer KVMs advertised as “supports DP++ / EDID emulation”.
  • Some KVMs force a low maximum mode (e.g. 1920×1080); verify it passes your native resolution.

8.5 A discrete GPU alternative

If you need more outputs or guaranteed HDMI:

  • Any cheap low-profile card (e.g. a GT 1030 / RX 6400 / Intel Arc A310) gives native HDMI/DP and sidesteps the iGPU entirely.
  • The ML10 Gen9 has one PCIe x16 slot (electrically x8/x16 depending on config) and a modest PSU; check power and clearance first.
  • On Windows Server this also often gets you a driver that actually installs, because discrete vendors ship server-adjacent drivers.

8.6 BIOS/firmware settings worth checking

In the ML10 Gen9 BIOS (F10 at boot):

  • Embedded Video / Onboard VGA — ensure it is enabled (there is no discrete GPU, so this should default on).
  • Primary display — if a discrete card is added, set which one POSTs.
  • Legacy vs UEFI video — UEFI generally gives a better GOP framebuffer; the reference machine boots UEFI.
  • BIOS version — the reference machine is on 1.010; newer BIOS revisions occasionally improve iGPU POST behaviour.

A BIOS update is not a fix for this bug, but it is worth having current firmware.

8.7 What not to do

  • Do not rely on nomodeset as a “fix”. It permanently caps you at the firmware resolution with no acceleration.
  • Do not disable the iGPU to “avoid conflicts” — you have no other GPU.
  • Do not buy a second passive adapter hoping a different brand behaves better; the mechanism is the same. Buy active.

8.8 Decision guide

flowchart TD
  A[No/ugly picture on ML10 Gen9] --> B{Can you replace the adapter?}
  B -- Yes --> C[Buy an ACTIVE DP->HDMI adapter]
  C --> D[Works on Linux, Windows, FreeBSD]
  B -- No / not yet --> E{Linux?}
  E -- Yes --> F[Use this repo's video= fix]
  E -- No --> G[Windows/other: install driver + registry/script force mode]
  D --> H[Done]
  F --> H
  G --> H

9. Troubleshooting

Work top to bottom. Almost every “still dark” case is one of: nomodeset still present, wrong connector name, wrong mode, or a passive adapter.

9.1 Quick checks

cat /proc/cmdline                     # is nomodeset gone? is video=<name>:<mode>e there?
grep -qw i915 /proc/modules           # is i915 loaded?
for c in /sys/class/drm/*/status; do echo "$(basename "$(dirname "$c")"): $(cat "$c")"; done
xrandr | grep connected
journalctl -k -b | grep -iE 'i915.*(fail|error|WARN)' | grep -vi AUX

9.2 Symptom → cause → fix

Symptom Likely cause Fix
modprobe i915 → “No such device”; only simpledrm nomodeset still on the cmdline Remove it, reboot (see 04)
“No signal” / monitor sleeps, nothing at all Connector not force-enabled, EDID missed Add video=<correct-name>:<mode>e
Signal present, black screen, cursor flickers You forced both DP-x and HDMI-A-x (same port) Force only the one matching the cable
Picture but 1024×768 / 640×480 Mode not forced; firmware framebuffer in use Force the native mode; check xrandr
Correct on one boot, wrong on the next EDID/bit-bang race at boot Keep the e suffix; consider an active adapter
Works at login screen, goes black after login Desktop picked a bad mode/scale Pin the mode (xrandr/Xorg/autostart)
i915 loads, no connector connected EDID not read at all (passive adapter) Use discover, then an active adapter
Wrong resolution only in the installer/live USB Live images may default to nomodeset Add the same video= token to the boot menu (e to edit, or Tab)
Flicker / random blanks at idle Skylake power features Keep i915.enable_dc=0 enable_psr=0 enable_fbc=0
Second monitor not detected Only one DDI active, or MST misconfig Enable the right second connector; keep enable_dp_mst=0 for a hub-free setup

9.3 (a) The screen is dark and I don’t know the connector name

This is the “chicken and egg” case: you cannot read /sys/class/drm names until i915 is running, but you cannot see anything when it is.

Option 1 — SSH (best)

Before rebooting, enable SSH so you can log in while the screen is dark:

sudo systemctl enable --now ssh
# note the IP:
ip -brief addr

Then boot without nomodeset (or use the toolkit’s discover entry) and, from another machine:

ssh you@<ip> 'for c in /sys/class/drm/*/status; do echo "$(basename "$(dirname "$c")"): $(cat "$c")"; done'

Whatever is connected is your connector name.

Option 2 — the toolkit’s discover entry

sudo ./i915-display-fix.sh discover            # adds a non-destructive GRUB entry
# reboot, pick "i915 DISCOVER - no nomodeset"
./i915-display-fix.sh detect                   # prints the connector + apply command

If even that stays dark, try:

sudo ./i915-display-fix.sh discover --force-all

--force-all force-enables every candidate port. It may still be black (multi connector conflict), but it lets you SSH in and read which connector reports connected/has an EDID. Then apply with that single connector.

Option 3 — guess from the port

If your cable is in the left DP port, try HDMI-A-1 first; the right port, try HDMI-A-2. You can pass both as separate attempts, rebooting between.

9.4 (b) “Signal but black screen, cursor flashes”

You are forcing two names for one port. Remove the video= tokens and keep only the one matching the cable:

-video=DP-1:1366x768@60e video=HDMI-A-1:1366x768@60e
+video=HDMI-A-1:1366x768@60e

Confirm in the log:

journalctl -b -1 -k | grep -i "handle_conflicting_encoders"

9.5 (c) Wrong resolution

Find the native mode:

xrandr                       # look at the '*' (current) and the list for the connected output
# or, without a desktop:
cat /sys/class/drm/card*-HDMI-A-1/modes | head

Set it live, then make it permanent:

xrandr --output HDMI-1 --mode 1366x768          # live test
# permanent: change the number in video=HDMI-A-1:1366x768@60e and re-run update-grub

9.6 (d) Recovery when the screen stays black

  1. Power-cycle. The GRUB menu (if it appears) lets you pick “Recovery - safe graphics (nomodeset)” or the distro’s recovery mode.
  2. If you cannot see the menu at all, force the recovery entry: - At the GRUB menu, press e, append nomodeset to the linux line, Ctrl-X/F10 to boot.
  3. Once in, revert:
sudo ./i915-display-fix.sh revert
sudo reboot
  1. Last resort: boot a live USB and edit /etc/default/grub on the installed system (mount the root partition, edit, chroot or just edit the file, then regenerate GRUB).

9.7 Diagnostic cheat-sheet

# GPU + driver
lspci -nnk | grep -A3 -iE 'vga|display'
# Kernel + cmdline
uname -r; cat /proc/cmdline
# Module state
grep -w i915 /proc/modules || echo "i915 not loaded"
# Connectors
for c in /sys/class/drm/*/status; do echo "$(basename "$(dirname "$c")"): $(cat "$c")"; done
# Modes per connector
cat /sys/class/drm/card*-HDMI-A-1/modes
# EDID presence
ls -l /sys/class/drm/card*-HDMI-A-1/edid
# Full DRM debug (verbose; needs drm.debug=0x1e on the cmdline)
journalctl -b -k | grep -iE 'i915|drm' | less

The automated collector is scripts/linux/i915-collect.sh.

9.8 Harmless log noise (do not chase)

intel_hdmi_set_edid: HDMI GMBUS EDID read failed, retry using GPIO bit-banging
failed to retrieve link info, disabling eDP
PSR condition failed: Port not supported
Reserved GGTT:[...] for use by error capture

These mean: EDID came in over bit-banging, there is no internal panel, and PSR isn’t applicable. They are expected on this hardware.

10. Verification

How to prove the fix worked, per platform. Run these after rebooting into the fixed configuration.

10.1 Linux — one-liners

# 1. Kernel: nomodeset is gone, the video= token is present
cat /proc/cmdline

# 2. The real driver is loaded
grep -qw i915 /proc/modules && echo "i915 OK" || echo "i915 MISSING"

# 3. The connector is connected and enabled at the right mode
for c in /sys/class/drm/*/status; do
  d=$(dirname "$c")
  echo "$(basename "$d"): $(cat "$c") enabled=$(cat "$d/enabled") mode=$(head -1 "$d/modes")"
done

# 4. Xorg sees it at the right resolution
xrandr | grep connected

# 5. Hardware acceleration (not llvmpipe)
glxinfo | grep -E 'OpenGL renderer|direct rendering'

Expected (reference machine):

HDMI-A-1: connected enabled=enabled mode=1366x768
HDMI-1 connected primary 1366x768+0+0
OpenGL renderer string: Mesa Intel(R) HD Graphics P530 (SKL GT2)
direct rendering: Yes

Or simply:

./scripts/linux/i915-display-fix.sh status

Automated pass/fail check

# fails loudly if nomodeset is still present or i915 is missing
! grep -qw nomodeset /proc/cmdline && grep -qw i915 /proc/modules \
  && echo "PASS" || echo "FAIL"

10.2 Finding your native resolution

# Preferred (first) mode the monitor advertises:
cat /sys/class/drm/card*-HDMI-A-1/modes | head -1

# Everything it supports:
cat /sys/class/drm/card*-HDMI-A-1/modes

# The raw EDID (decode with edid-decode if installed):
ls -l /sys/class/drm/card*-HDMI-A-1/edid
edid-decode /sys/class/drm/card*-HDMI-A-1/edid | grep -i preferred -A2

The first mode in modes is the monitor’s preferred/native mode — use it in the video= token.

10.3 Windows / Server

Get-CimInstance Win32_VideoController |
  Select-Object Name, DriverVersion, CurrentHorizontalResolution,
                CurrentVerticalResolution, CurrentRefreshRate

# confirm it is not the basic adapter:
Get-PnpDevice -Class Display | Format-Table Status, FriendlyName, InstanceId

Good: Intel(R) HD Graphics ... at your native resolution, not Microsoft Basic Display Adapter.

The provided tools:

powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\windows\Get-GraphicsInfo.ps1
DisplayFix.exe --current

10.4 FreeBSD

sysctl kern.vty                       # should say vt
kldstat | grep i915kms
pciconf -lv | grep -A4 vgapci
# under X:
xrandr | grep connected

10.5 Performance sanity check

A properly driven display has hardware acceleration. If glxinfo says llvmpipe (Linux) or Windows shows the Basic Display Adapter, the fix is not complete even if the resolution looks right.

# Linux: should NOT say llvmpipe / softpipe
glxinfo | grep -i 'renderer'

# Quick OpenGL capability
glxinfo | grep 'OpenGL version'

10.6 What “success” looks like

Check Expected
/proc/cmdline no nomodeset; has video=<connector>:<WxH>@<Hz>e
Driver i915 loaded (Linux) / Intel driver (Windows)
Connector exactly one connected, enabled
Current mode monitor’s native resolution
Renderer Intel GPU, hardware accelerated
Stability no flicker / blanking over several minutes idle

11. Reference

11.1 Kernel command line parameters used

Parameter Values Meaning
nomodeset (presence) Blocks DRM/KMS drivers (sets video_firmware_drivers_only()). Remove it.
video=<conn>:<WxH>[@Hz][e] see §11.2 Force-enable an output and its mode.
i915.enable_dc= 0/1/2 Display C-states (DC5/DC6). 0 = off (stable).
i915.enable_psr= 0/1 Panel Self Refresh. 0 = off.
i915.enable_fbc= 0/1 Frame Buffer Compression. 0 = off.
i915.enable_dp_mst= 0/1 DP Multi-Stream Transport. 0 = off.
i915.disable_power_well= 0/1/-1 0 = keep power wells always on.
drm.debug= hex bitmask DRM debug categories (see §11.4).
log_buf_len= e.g. 16M Enlarge the kernel log ring (for verbose debug).
quiet — Suppress most boot messages.
splash — Graphical boot splash.

11.2 video= syntax in full

video=<connector>:<xres>x<yres>[@<refresh>][<options>]
  • <connector> — DRM connector name: DP-1, HDMI-A-1, eDP-1, VGA-1, … Use the name from /sys/class/drm/.
  • <refresh> — optional vertical refresh in Hz, e.g. @60.
  • <options> — one or more of:
Suffix Meaning
e Force-enable the output even if the driver thinks it is disconnected. This is the key suffix for this bug.
d Force-disable the output.
D Enable with digital (TMDS) signalling — useful to force an HDMI/DVI encoder.
m Use mode with margins.
i Interlaced.

Examples:

video=HDMI-A-1:1366x768@60e      # force 1366x768@60 on HDMI-A-1, even if "disconnected"
video=DP-1:d                     # force-disable DP-1
video=HDMI-A-1:1920x1080@60eD    # force digital + 1080p

You can list several video= tokens, but do not force both names of the same physical port (see 03).

11.3 Connector name ↔ X output name

DRM (kernel) Xorg (xrandr) Type
HDMI-A-1 HDMI-1 HDMI/DP++ in TMDS mode
DP-1 DP-1 native DisplayPort
eDP-1 eDP-1 internal panel
VGA-1 VGA-1 analog

HDMI-A-2, DP-2, … correspond to the next physical port.

11.4 drm.debug bitmask

Bit Category
0x01 DRM_UT_CORE
0x02 DRM_UT_DRIVER
0x04 DRM_UT_KMS (connector/EDID/modeset — the useful one)
0x08 DRM_UT_PRIME
0x10 DRM_UT_ATOMIC
0x1e DRIVER+KMS+PRIME+ATOMIC (what this repo used)

Debug messages are rate-limited and verbose; turn them off (remove drm.debug) once you are done.

11.5 Useful commands

# DRM state
cat /sys/class/drm/card*-*/status
cat /sys/class/drm/card*-*/modes
cat /sys/class/drm/card*-*/enabled

# Xorg
xrandr --verbose
xrandr --output HDMI-1 --mode 1366x768 --rate 60
cvt 1366 768 60              # generate a modeline
gtf 1366 768 60

# Kernel / module
modinfo i915
for p in /sys/module/i915/parameters/*; do echo "$(basename $p)=$(cat $p)"; done

# Boot
bootctl status                # systemd-boot
grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg

11.6 Glossary

Term Meaning
KMS Kernel Mode Setting — the kernel programs the display controller.
i915 Linux kernel driver for Intel integrated graphics.
nomodeset Kernel flag that disables KMS; leaves the firmware framebuffer.
EDID Monitor capability block read over DDC/I²C.
DDC / DDC-CI Display Data Channel (the I²C bus carrying EDID).
GMBUS Intel’s hardware I²C controller for DDC.
Bit-banging Software-toggling the DDC lines when GMBUS fails (slow).
DP++ Dual-mode DisplayPort: can output native DP or TMDS (HDMI/DVI).
DDI Digital Display Interface — the physical Intel display port block.
DDC see above
CRTC Display controller / scanout pipe.
PHY The electrical layer of a display port.
PSR Panel Self Refresh (power saving).
FBC Frame Buffer Compression.
MST Multi-Stream Transport (daisy-chaining DP displays).
DCH Declarative Componentized Hardware — modern Windows driver model.
WDDM Windows Display Driver Model.

11.7 File locations (Linux)

Path Purpose
/etc/default/grub GRUB defaults (edit here)
/boot/grub/grub.cfg generated GRUB (Debian/Arch)
/boot/grub2/grub.cfg generated GRUB (Fedora/openSUSE)
/etc/grub.d/ scripts that generate menu entries (never put backups here)
/boot/loader/entries/*.conf systemd-boot entries
/sys/class/drm/ live connector state
/var/backups/i915-display-fix/ backups made by this repo’s toolkit
/etc/X11/xorg.conf.d/ Xorg snippets (mode pinning)

12. FAQ

Q: Is my ML10 Gen9’s iGPU actually supported? Yes. The HD Graphics P530 (8086:191d) is fully supported by Linux i915 and by the Windows Intel graphics driver. HP does not ship a Windows Server driver for it, which is why it “looks” unsupported.

Q: Why does nomodeset “work” then? Because it does not use the GPU at all — it uses the BIOS’s simple framebuffer (simpledrm). That is why you are stuck at 1024×768 with no acceleration.

Q: Can I fix this without rebooting? No. nomodeset is read once at boot. Live modprobe i915 fails while it is set.

Q: Do I really need the i915.enable_* flags? Usually only video=<conn>:<WxH>@<Hz>e (and removing nomodeset) is required. The flags are conservative stability tweaks for Skylake; keep them if you saw flicker, drop them if you prefer default power behaviour and it still works.

Q: Why do I have to name HDMI-A-1 when the port is a DisplayPort? Because a DP++ port is dual-mode. In HDMI/DVI mode the kernel exposes it under the HDMI-A-x name. DP-1 and HDMI-A-1 are the same physical port.

Q: I forced both and got a black screen with a cursor. Why? Two connectors on one port fight over the shared encoder (handle_conflicting_encoders), so the driver keeps disabling your monitor. Force only one.

Q: Can I use my monitor’s full 1920×1080? Yes, if the monitor and adapter support it. Put the native mode in the token: video=HDMI-A-1:1920x1080@60e. Verify the mode exists: cat /sys/class/drm/card*-HDMI-A-1/modes.

Q: Will this survive kernel updates? Yes. /etc/default/grub is static, and update-grub/grub2-mkconfig regenerates from it for every installed kernel. The optional custom recovery entry hardcodes the kernel of the day; re-run apply after a major upgrade, or rely on your distro’s built-in recovery entry.

Q: What about Secure Boot? The fix does not touch boot signing; it only changes the kernel command line. It works with Secure Boot enabled. The Windows .exe approach is unaffected.

Q: Does this help on Windows? Not directly. On Windows install the Intel driver and use an active adapter; the video= concept does not exist there. See docs/06-windows-server.md.

Q: Is a passive adapter really the problem? It is the root of the EDID failure. Passive DP→HDMI/DVI plugs do not regenerate DDC. An active adapter removes the need for the software workaround.

Q: I only see 640×480. Is that a different bug? No. It is the same: without EDID the driver/OS falls back to a safe low mode. Force the mode, then consider an active adapter.

Q: Can I disable nomodeset but keep text-only boot? Yes — use nomodeset only for the recovery entry; the normal entry should not have it. That is exactly what this repo sets up.

Q: How do I go back? sudo ./scripts/linux/i915-display-fix.sh revert, or restore the .bak of /etc/default/grub and update-grub. A recovery GRUB entry is always left in place.

Q: Why did my GRUB menu get a duplicate/garbled entry after editing? Because a *.bak file was left inside /etc/grub.d/, which GRUB executes. Keep backups elsewhere (the toolkit uses /var/backups/i915-display-fix/).

Q: Will this work on a monitor with DisplayPort directly (no adapter)? Yes, and it is the best case. You may not even need the video= force; plain nomodeset-removal is likely enough.

Q: Is there a risk of bricking the display permanently? No. All changes are file-based and reversible, and a nomodeset recovery entry is always available. Even in the worst case you reach a console with a live USB.
